_what: Possible patterns: the same kind of thing as the patterns beside them, but ones nobody has proved yet. Each is told as a continuous rundown for a reader new to the subject - what is probably happening, why that is likely, which proved cases sit nearest to it, and what would turn it into cases or knock it down. None of them is evidence. No person or company is named except in the cases already proved.

items.title: The same drafting shops writing the statutes of many governments at once
items.claim: The text of investment, mining and tax laws is probably supplied to many governments from one small set of drafting shops and model texts, so a rule written by a few unelected people is likely in force in countries that never debated it.
items.rule: The copying is measured one level up. A study of more than 600 bilateral investment treaties found the average treaty takes roughly 50 to 65 per cent of its wording from an earlier one, and over 100 copy 80 per cent or more. The map proves the same movement at the level of statutes: industry-written model bills were copied into about 10,000 United States state bills, and a corporate-and-legislator forum drafted an immigration law that was then enacted. Where text travels by copying, the people who wrote the model also advise the ministry that enacts it.
items.conditions: A bill is often drafted by a few people in one ministry or legislative office, with an outside adviser alongside. The adviser's instructions and drafts are not published, and in most countries there is no register of who wrote a bill. Model texts are public; the drafting advice behind each enactment is not.
items.documented: Nearest on the map: 'ALEC Exposed: 850 corporate-drafted model bills published' and 'Industry-written model bills copied into 10,000 US state bills', both proved. Also 'ALEC meeting drafted Arizona's SB 1070 immigration law', and the Big Four accountants seconded to the Treasury to help write tax law. Nothing proved yet shows one drafting shop supplying the same operative text to several countries.
items.would_show: Two or more national statutes whose operative provisions match one private model, with an engagement letter, secondment record or drafting file showing the same adviser wrote each.
items.would_refute: Ministry drafting files for the closest-matching statutes showing the text was written in-house, with the model used only as a reference and the adviser excluded from drafting.
story: When a country rewrites the law on who owns its minerals, or on what an investor may sue it for, the words are usually typed by a handful of people in one ministry office. Often one of them is not a civil servant at all, but an adviser flown in and paid by a lender, a law firm or an industry body, and he arrives with a draft already written. The probable result is that the same rule, written by people no voter has ever heard of, is in force in dozens of countries that never really debated it.

The copying has been measured. Researchers compared more than 600 investment treaties and found that since 1990 the average one takes between half and two-thirds of its wording straight from an earlier treaty, and over a hundred of them copy eighty per cent or more. Ordinary national law moves the same way. A forum where corporations sat down with state legislators in the United States produced model bills that were copied into roughly ten thousand state bills; 850 of those drafts became public when the operation leaked, and one of its meetings produced the text of Arizona's SB 1070 immigration law.

What keeps it out of sight is that almost nothing about the drafting is published. The model texts are public, the advice is not, and most countries keep no register of who actually wrote a bill, so the adviser's instructions and his successive drafts stay inside the building. The closest proved case runs the same way round: accountants from the Big Four firms were seconded into a national Treasury and helped write tax law, while their firms advised the companies that law would fall on.

Nobody has yet set two countries' statutes side by side, matched the operative sections to a single private model, and produced the engagement letter or secondment record showing the same firm advised both ministries. That comparison has not been done.

items.title: The largest shareholders advising the regulators that oversee them
items.claim: Firms that hold the largest stakes in regulated banks and companies are probably also advising the central banks and finance ministries that set the rules those stakes live under, in several countries at the same time, so one private firm may sit on both sides of the same decision.
items.rule: The structure is documented. One asset manager's advisory arm was created in 2008 to advise governments and central banks, and went on to advise the United States Federal Reserve and several European central banks. Its risk platform was reported to analyse about $21.6 trillion of assets by 2020. Under the Federal Reserve's 2020 facility terms, staff could move from that work to client-facing work after a two-week cooling-off period. The map proves the same arrangement elsewhere: a founder of a finance firm was given a desk inside a government department while the firm was in dealings with it.
items.conditions: These engagements are often awarded without open competition and the contracts are not published. Members of the United States Congress asked in 2020 for the contract terms and conflict-of-interest procedures. The information the adviser sees, such as bank balance sheets under supervisory review or an intervention before it is announced, reaches no other market participant. The safeguards are set and audited by the firm itself.
items.documented: Nearest on the map: 'Greensill Capital: founder inside Downing Street, civil servant on its side', and 'Banker offered Puerto Rico's governor campaign cash to replace his regulator', both proved. Nothing proved yet ties an asset manager's advisory work to a decision that moved its own holdings.
items.would_show: A supervisory, purchase or intervention decision where the record shows the adviser's own holdings or products were affected and its staff drafted or recommended the option chosen.
items.would_refute: Contracts and internal access logs showing the information barriers held, with no traffic between the advisory team and the investment side on the decisions at issue.
story: A small number of asset managers now hold a slice of nearly every large bank and listed company in the world. The same firms are also hired, for a fee, to advise the central banks and finance ministries that decide the rules those holdings live under. The probable position is that in several countries at once a single private firm sits on both sides of the same decision: it owns the thing being regulated, and it is in the room helping to write the regulation.

The structure is not hidden. One asset manager set up an arm in 2008 for the specific purpose of advising governments and central banks, and it went on to advise the United States Federal Reserve and a series of European central banks; by 2020 its risk software was reported to be analysing around twenty-one trillion dollars of assets. When the Federal Reserve ran an emergency corporate credit programme that year, the published terms allowed the firm's staff to move from that work back to serving its own clients after a two-week pause.

What makes it workable is the paperwork nobody sees. These jobs have repeatedly been handed out without open competition and the contracts have not been published; members of Congress wrote in 2020 to ask for the terms and the conflict-of-interest rules and did not get them. The adviser meanwhile sees things no other investor sees, such as the state of a bank's books under supervisory review, or the design of an intervention before it is announced. The barriers that are supposed to contain that information are set by the firm and audited by the firm.

The smaller version of this is proved twice over. The founder of a finance company was given a desk inside Downing Street, with a civil servant working on the company's side, and a banker in Puerto Rico offered the governor campaign money to replace his own regulator. What has not been produced is a single decision — a supervisory call, a purchase, a rescue — where the record shows the adviser's own holdings were among those affected and its staff recommended the option chosen.

items.title: Companies voting the technical standards that become law
items.claim: In the technical committees whose texts national law then adopts by reference, the voting experts are probably in large part employed by the firms the standard governs, so rules with the force of law are likely drafted by the industries they bind.
items.rule: The map proves the mechanism at a standards body. Partners of a software maker joined national committees to vote its document format into the international standard, and a national intelligence agency steered a weakened encryption standard through the standards bodies. The bodies are open to industry by design, and their texts become binding when a government adopts them by reference. A committee that no government controls, whose text becomes law, is the same shape as a lobbyist drafting a bill, which the map proves elsewhere.
items.conditions: Committees run to a few dozen members and are staffed through national standards bodies, many funded by selling the standards they help write. The employer of each voting member, and who paid for each delegate, is generally not stated in the published standard. Drafts and ballots go to members, not to the public.
items.documented: Nearest on the map: 'Microsoft partners joined national committees to vote its format into ISO' and 'NSA steered a weakened encryption standard through NIST and ISO', both proved. Nothing proved yet ties a standard to a member's employer in a way that decided the outcome.
items.would_show: A standard later adopted into national law where the committee record shows the drafting members were employed by firms whose product the text admits or excludes, and a competitor's objection was voted down by those members.
items.would_refute: Committee rosters and ballot records showing government, academic and consumer members held the deciding votes on the standards in question.
story: Most people never learn how a technical standard becomes law. A government writes a single line into its rulebook saying that equipment, or a building, or a medical device must meet standard number such-and-such, and from that moment the text of a private committee has the force of law. The committees that write those texts are open to the industries they govern, and the probable position is that the people holding the votes are in large part employed by the firms the standard is meant to bind.

It has already happened twice inside these same bodies. A software maker's commercial partners joined national standards committees and voted its document format through to international adoption. Separately, a national intelligence agency steered a deliberately weakened encryption standard through the standards process, which is the same mechanism turned to a different purpose: get your people into the committee and the committee's output carries your preference out into everyone else's law.

The conditions favour it. A committee may be a few dozen people and a working group fewer. Participation runs through national standards bodies, many of which are funded by selling the very standards they help write. The employer of each voting member is generally not printed in the published standard, drafts and ballots circulate only to members, and the finished text is usually sold rather than published, so the public pays to read a rule it is bound by.

What is missing is a standard later written into national law, with a committee record showing that the members who drafted it worked for the firms whose product the text lets in or keeps out, and a competitor's objection voted down by those same members.

items.title: The judges and advocates of investment disputes being one circle
items.claim: The tribunals that decide whether a state may regulate an investor are probably staffed largely from a small circle of people who also argue cases before the same tribunals, so the judges and the advocates in this system may be substantially the same people.
items.rule: This is counted, not supposed. A survey of 1,077 investment arbitrations found 509, or 47 per cent, involved arbitrators who were at the same time acting as counsel or expert in other cases. The system's own rule-writers treat the overlap as a defect: the UNCITRAL working group agreed a code of conduct in 2023 with cooling-off periods of one to three years. The map proves that arbitration itself is a place where influence is bought: a company bribed a government lawyer during an arbitration.
items.conditions: A tribunal is three people, one chosen by each side and one agreed between them, drawn from a small pool of repeat appointees and paid by the parties. Hearings and many awards are confidential. Until the 2023 code, disclosure of concurrent roles was left largely to the arbitrator.
items.documented: Nearest on the map: 'P&ID bribed a Nigerian government lawyer during arbitration', and 'Leaks say arbitrators weighed bribery of Kazakh officials over Karacha', both proved as bribery in arbitration rather than as double-hatting. Honest gap: no proved case of an arbitrator with concurrent roles shaping an award.
items.would_show: An award where an arbitrator was concurrently counsel for a party, or for its affiliate, in another case on the same treaty provision, and did not disclose it at the time.
items.would_refute: Disclosure records across the same case set showing concurrent roles were declared, and party challenges were heard and ruled on in the closest cases.
story: A company that dislikes a country's new law can, under thousands of investment treaties, sue that country for compensation. The case is not heard in a public court. It goes to a tribunal of three private individuals, one chosen by each side and one agreed between them, and they can order a state to pay hundreds of millions. The probable position is that the people who sit as judges in this system are drawn from the same small circle of lawyers who argue the cases, so that the bench and the bar are substantially the same few dozen people.

This one has been counted rather than guessed at. A survey of 1,077 investment arbitrations found that 509 of them, forty-seven per cent, involved an arbitrator who was at the same time acting as counsel or as a paid expert in other cases. The people who run the system treat the overlap as a defect, not a theory: a United Nations working group agreed a code of conduct in 2023 imposing cooling-off periods of one to three years, and some newer treaties ban the practice outright.

Everything about the setting protects it. Appointments are repeat business from a small pool, the parties pay the arbitrators' fees, hearings and many awards are confidential, and until that 2023 code it was largely left to the arbitrator himself to disclose what else he was working on.

The map's own cases stop short of the claim. They prove that arbitration is a place where influence gets bought — a company bribed a Nigerian government lawyer during an arbitration, and leaked material describes arbitrators weighing the bribery of Kazakh officials in a dispute over the Karachaganak field — but it holds no case of an arbitrator's second hat shaping an award. What would be needed is an award where the arbitrator was at the same time counsel for a party or its affiliate in another case on the same treaty clause, and did not say so.

items.title: Suppliers and private funders holding seats over what global health buys
items.claim: The bodies that set global health priorities and buy vaccines at scale are probably giving governing seats and funding leverage to the suppliers and private funders who gain from what is bought, so part of the purchaser's agenda may be set by the sellers.
items.rule: The arrangement is published and can be read from the budget. More than 80 per cent of the World Health Organization's budget is voluntary money, and in 2024 to 2025 the largest contributor was a private foundation at about 13 per cent of that. A vaccine alliance was second at about 11.6 per cent, and its board gives permanent seats to the same foundation and to the vaccine industry. The map already proves tobacco companies working inside the WHO. This is the purchasing layer of the same arrangement.
items.conditions: Priorities are set by boards of a few dozen people deciding by consensus or two-thirds majority. Where a body depends on one donor for a large share of its money, withdrawal is a sanction that needs no vote. Supply agreements, prices and volume commitments are routinely confidential.
items.documented: Nearest on the map: 'Tobacco companies secretly worked to undermine WHO from inside', proved as industry inside a rule-making body. Nothing proved yet ties a board seat to a purchase decision.
items.would_show: A procurement or priority decision where the record shows a board member's own product was selected and that member took part in the vote.
items.would_refute: Board minutes and recusal records showing industry and funder seats were excluded from votes on the products they supply.
story: The bodies that decide which vaccines and medicines the poorer half of the world receives, and that buy them by the hundred million dose, are not funded the way people assume. The probable position is that the suppliers who sell the product and the private funders who pay for it also hold seats at the table where it is decided what gets bought, which would put part of the buyer's agenda in the hands of the sellers.

This can be read straight off the budget. More than eighty per cent of the World Health Organization's money is voluntary contributions rather than dues, and in the 2024 to 2025 budget the single largest contributor was a private foundation at about thirteen per cent of that voluntary money. A vaccine alliance was the second largest at around eleven and a half per cent, and that alliance's own board hands permanent seats to the same foundation and allocated seats to the vaccine industry.

The leverage does not need a vote to work. Priorities are set by boards of a few dozen people deciding by consensus or two-thirds majority, and where an organisation depends on one donor for a large slice of its budget, the mere possibility of withdrawal shapes what gets proposed. The supply agreements, the prices paid and the volumes committed are routinely confidential, so the public cannot check what its money bought.

An industry has already been caught working inside this institution: tobacco companies were found to have operated inside the WHO to undermine it. What has not been shown is the purchasing version — a procurement or priority decision where the record shows a board member's own product was selected and that member took part in the decision.

items.title: Central bankers and the banks they supervise meeting in closed rooms
items.claim: Decisions on money and bank supervision are probably shaped in invitation-only forums where the officials who take them and the bankers they supervise meet without published minutes, moving part of policy out of any record the public can reach.
items.rule: An official watchdog has already found this kind of overlap improper. In January 2018 the European Ombudsman found that a central bank president's membership of an invitation-only bankers' club amounted to maladministration, because members included directors of banks the bank supervised. She recommended he suspend the membership and that future presidents not join. The map proves the older form: bankers secretly drafted the Federal Reserve plan at Jekyll Island, and bank owners bribed a central bank chief in Latvia.
items.conditions: Membership is by invitation and meetings are confidential. Attendance may appear in an official diary, but agendas, papers and discussion do not. The firms in the room are often the ones whose capital, resolution and liquidity support the officials decide.
items.documented: Nearest on the map: 'Bankers secretly drafted the Federal Reserve plan at Jekyll Island', and 'Latvian bank's owners bribed central bank chief and ECB member', both proved. Honest gap: no proved case of a closed-forum meeting shaping a specific rate or supervisory decision.
items.would_show: A supervisory or policy position that changed after a closed meeting, with notes, correspondence or testimony tying the change to what was said there.
items.would_refute: Published agendas and summaries showing the meetings dealt only in general analysis, with matters concerning members' own firms excluded.
story: Decisions about interest rates, and about which banks are sound enough to carry on, are taken by a very small number of officials. Some of those officials belong to invitation-only forums where they sit, in private and without published minutes, alongside executives of the banks they supervise. The probable position is that part of monetary and supervisory policy is shaped in those rooms, where no record exists that the public can ever reach.

An official watchdog has already called this improper. In January 2018 the European Ombudsman concluded that a central bank president's membership of one such invitation-only bankers' club amounted to maladministration, precisely because its members included directors of banks that his institution supervised. She recommended that he give up the membership and that his successors never take it up.

The older and blunter forms of this are already proved. The plan that became the Federal Reserve was drafted in secret by bankers on Jekyll Island, at a meeting arranged to look like a duck-shooting trip. In Latvia, the owners of a bank bribed the central bank governor, who also sat on the European Central Bank's council. The modern version needs no bribe, because the banker and the supervisor are already in the same room by invitation.

What is missing is the link between a meeting and an outcome: a supervisory or policy position that changed after one of these gatherings, with notes, correspondence or testimony tying the change to what was said there.

items.title: The firms that sell tax structures writing the laws that allow them
items.claim: In jurisdictions that supply secrecy and tax residence to the rest of the world, statutes are probably written in large part by the private firms that then sell the structures those statutes permit, so the law may be drafted by its own customers.
items.rule: Legal scholarship describes interested private parties working closely with the legislatures of small offshore jurisdictions, partners of offshore firms holding government posts, and jurisdictions converting lawmaking authority into revenue. Leak-based reporting found that more than 300 lawyers at one global firm had advised a state or international body on tax or anti-corruption legislation, while the firm was connected to more than 440 offshore companies. The map proves the same pairing in a different setting: accounting-firm staff seconded to a national Treasury to help write tax law.
items.conditions: A small legislature may have no standing drafting office, so an outside draft is often the only draft. The instructing client and fee are not published. The firm that drafts may also incorporate and administer the entities the statute creates, so one firm writes the rule and sells the product.
items.documented: Nearest on the map: 'Big Four accountants seconded to the Treasury to help write tax law', proved as placement inside the body that writes the rule. Honest gap: no proved case of an offshore firm drafting the statute under which it then sells structures.
items.would_show: A statute or amendment whose drafting file, legislative record or billing shows a private firm wrote it, where that firm also sells the structures the statute enables.
items.would_refute: Drafting records showing the text came from a government law office or a multilateral adviser with no commercial interest in the structures created.
story: A dozen small jurisdictions supply the rest of the world with secrecy, shell companies and tax residence. Their company and trust laws are unusually well built for that trade. The probable explanation is that those laws are largely written by the private firms that then sell the structures the laws permit, which would mean the statute book of these places is drafted by its own customers.

Some firms say so themselves: legislative drafting is listed as a practice area by the largest law firm in at least one such jurisdiction, alongside trusts, funds and company administration. Leaked records showed that more than three hundred lawyers at a single global firm had advised a government or an international body on tax or anti-corruption legislation, while that same firm was connected to more than four hundred offshore companies. Academic work on these places describes interested private parties working hand in hand with tiny legislatures, firm partners holding seats in government, and small states turning the power to make law into a revenue stream.

The mechanics are mundane. A legislature of a few dozen members may have no permanent drafting office, so an outside draft is not merely welcome, it is the only draft. Who instructed the drafter and what he was paid are not published. And the firm that writes the rule frequently also incorporates the companies, administers the trusts and acts as registered agent, so one set of partners writes the law, sells the product and keeps the records.

The proved case closest to this is narrower: accounting-firm staff seconded into a national Treasury to help write tax law. What is missing is a statute or amendment whose drafting file, legislative record or billing shows a private firm wrote it, where that firm also sells the structures it enables.

items.title: Former intelligence officers selling their service's methods to foreign clients
items.claim: Former officers of national intelligence services are probably working for foreign states and private clients in numbers large enough to matter, carrying the access and methods of the services they left.
items.rule: One case is proved in the form of a United States prosecution agreement. Three former intelligence and military employees ran hacking operations for a foreign government through a company from 2016 to 2019, paid $1.685 million between them, surrendered their clearances and accepted employment limits. Enforcement officials then warned other former employees publicly, which implies the pool is larger than the three charged. The map proves the state-to-state form of the same thing: a state's own service running the access it holds.
items.conditions: These engagements are commercial contracts with non-disclosure terms. Export control is the main legal handle, and it reaches tools more readily than people. There is no public register of where former officers of most services go. The client can classify the work it commissions.
items.documented: Honest zero. The map holds no case of former officers selling their service's methods to a foreign client. Nearest proved: 'CIA and BND secretly owned Swiss cipher firm Crypto AG', which shows a service inside a commercial vendor. The rule above rests on the public prosecution record outside the map.
items.would_show: A second state's enforcement action or court record showing former officers of its own service worked for a foreign client against its interests or its allies.
items.would_refute: Post-employment records showing former officers' foreign work was licensed and supervised, leaving the case isolated rather than typical.
story: A government trains someone for years to break into other people's systems, run informants and read other states' mail. Then that person resigns. The skills, the methods and the contacts leave with him, and there is a market. The probable position is that former officers of national intelligence services are now working for foreign governments and private clients in numbers large enough to matter.

One instance is proved, and its shape is general. In 2021 the United States settled with three men who had served in its intelligence community or military and had then spent the years from 2016 to 2019 running hacking operations for a foreign government through a private company. They paid just under 1.7 million dollars between them, surrendered every security clearance they held and accepted limits on who they may work for. What matters as much as the case is what officials did next: they issued a public warning aimed at other former employees, which is not the act of people who believe they have found all of it.

The trade is protected by its paperwork. These are commercial contracts under foreign law with confidentiality clauses. Export control is the main legal handle and it grips tools far better than it grips people. There is no public register of where former officers of most services end up, and the client is a state that can classify the work it has commissioned.

The map holds nothing on this, and says so. Its nearest case is the mirror image rather than the thing itself: the CIA and West Germany's BND secretly owned Crypto AG, the Swiss firm that sold cipher machines to around a hundred governments, and read what those governments wrote — a service hidden inside a company, rather than a company staffed by a service's alumni. What would turn this into a case is a second country's prosecution or court record showing its own former officers collecting against it, or against its allies, for a foreign client.

items.title: Suppliers of national identity and payment systems inside the bodies that choose them
items.claim: The companies that build national identity and payment systems are probably inside the ministries and programmes that choose and mandate those systems, so a few suppliers may set the terms on which large populations are enrolled, identified and paid.
items.rule: The map proves the purchasing end of this repeatedly. A multinational paid over $100 million to officials for a $1 billion ID-card deal, and contractors paid a national legislative leader. A Belgian firm was sent to trial over a cut of each passport issued in one country. Identity systems have few qualified bidders, and the lender programmes that fund them publish technical guidance that names vendor lock-in as a risk in borrowing countries.
items.conditions: A national identity decision is usually taken by one commission or ministry, under a single integrator contract running for years. Biometric matching, card supply and payment switching each have few qualified bidders. Contract terms, pricing and data-ownership clauses are often unpublished.
items.documented: Nearest on the map: 'Siemens paid over $100m to Argentine officials for a $1bn ID-card deal', and 'e-KTP contractors paid Indonesia's House Speaker Setya Novanto', both proved as bribery in procurement. Honest gap: no proved case of a supplier writing the specification it then wins.
items.would_show: An identity or payment mandate where the specification was written by a bidder, or the deciding official was employed by one before or after the award.
items.would_refute: Procurement files for the largest such programmes showing specifications written in-house and competitive awards, with deciding officials unconnected to any bidder.
story: Across much of the world a person's ability to vote, be treated, cross a border or be paid a benefit now runs through one national identity system and one payment rail. A handful of companies build them. The probable position is that those companies are inside the ministries and programmes that choose the systems and then make them compulsory, which would let a few suppliers set the terms on which whole populations are enrolled, identified and paid.

The buying end of this is proved on the map repeatedly. A multinational paid more than a hundred million dollars to officials to win a one-billion-dollar national identity card contract in Argentina. Contractors on Indonesia's electronic identity card paid the Speaker of its parliament. A Belgian firm was sent to trial over taking a cut of every passport issued in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The pattern here is the step beyond bribery: not paying for the contract, but being inside the body that writes what the contract must contain.

The conditions are ideal for it. One commission or ministry usually decides, under a single integrator contract that runs for years and then renews. Worldwide there are few credible bidders for biometric matching, card production or payment switching, so the shortlist is short before anyone writes a specification. Contract terms, unit prices and the clauses saying who owns the data often go unpublished. The lenders funding these programmes name vendor lock-in as a risk in their own guidance, having watched it happen.
What is not yet shown is a mandate where the technical specification was written by a bidder, or where the official who made the decision worked for one before or after the award.

items.title: Private forums picking who will govern, a cohort at a time
items.claim: A small number of private forums are probably selecting and cultivating cohorts of rising politicians, officials, judges and executives who then hold office across many countries at once, which would mean part of who governs is decided by invitation rather than by any electorate.
items.rule: The map proves this shape completely, in an older form that nobody disputes. A private network built on one man's mining fortune selected young men, placed them in colonial administration and the Foreign Office, and its members then drafted constitutional arrangements for India and pressed South Africa into union from inside the government. A modern policy foundation wrote a programme for an incoming administration and then supplied the people who staffed it. Selecting people and placing them is a method with a track record, and the forums that run it today publish their cohort lists while publishing nothing about what is asked of alumni afterwards.
items.conditions: Membership of these programmes is by invitation and the selection criteria are not published. Alumni hold office in dozens of countries simultaneously, often in finance ministries, central banks and regulators, and no register of interests anywhere requires an official to declare that a private forum selected and trained him. The forums are constituted as charities or foundations, so their internal deliberations are not public records.
items.documented: Proved on the map: 'Milner's Kindergarten pressed for South African union from inside', 'Round Table study group with India Office officials drafted dyarchy', and both Heritage items - the 1981 Mandate for Leadership with most of its proposals acted on, and Project 2025's authors staffing the administration they wrote for. Honest gap: the map holds no case involving a present-day forum's alumni programme.
items.would_show: A decision taken by an office-holder on the instruction, request or coordinated prompting of the forum that selected him, shown in correspondence, minutes or testimony - not merely a count of alumni holding posts.
items.would_refute: Alumni lists set against appointment records showing no more placement than comparable professional networks produce, and forum papers showing no contact with alumni once they take office.
story: Every year a handful of private forums choose a few dozen people in their thirties and forties - politicians on the way up, central bank staff, prosecutors, officers, executives - and bring them into a programme. Ten years later a striking number of them are finance ministers, regulators and heads of state. The probable position is that part of the answer to who governs is settled by invitation, in rooms nobody can attend, well before any voter is asked.

The older version of this is proved on the map and nobody seriously disputes it. A network funded out of one man's mining fortune picked promising young men, placed them through colonial administration and the Foreign Office, and its members went on to draft constitutional machinery for India and to press South Africa into union from inside its own government. The same method appears in a modern form: a policy foundation wrote the programme for an incoming administration, and then the people who had written it took the jobs that would carry it out.

What is missing from the modern version is anything about the afterlife. The forums publish their cohort lists; they publish nothing about what is asked of an alumnus once he holds office. No register of interests in any country requires an official to disclose that a private body selected and trained him, and the forums are constituted as charities, so their internal papers are not public records.

To become a case this needs more than a headcount of alumni in cabinets, which proves only that ambitious people join things. It needs one decision taken on the forum's instruction or coordinated prompting, visible in correspondence, minutes or testimony.

items.title: Intelligence officers on the staff of the bodies that inspect and feed the world
items.claim: Intelligence services are probably running officers under cover as ordinary staff of United Nations agencies, weapons inspectorates and relief bodies, which would put the institutions the world relies on for neutral findings partly inside national intelligence systems.
items.rule: The map proves both halves separately. A police spy for the apartheid state became deputy director of an aid fund in Geneva. A Chinese official working inside the United Nations says he had a Uyghur leader removed from a UN forum at Beijing's request. And two services jointly and secretly owned the Swiss firm that sold cipher machines to around a hundred governments, then read what those governments sent - which shows the appetite for sitting inside a trusted neutral body is not hypothetical. The access on offer here is better than most espionage buys: inspectors enter sites no spy can reach, and relief staff travel where armies cannot.
items.conditions: These bodies recruit from member states and, in practice, often accept the candidate a government puts forward. Vetting is light and belongs to the organisation, which has no counter-intelligence arm of its own. Staff enjoy privileges and immunities, so the host country frequently cannot investigate them. Inspection findings and the identity of the people who produced them are routinely withheld for the staff's own safety.
items.documented: Proved on the map: 'Apartheid police spy became deputy director of a Geneva aid fund', 'Chinese UN official says he had Uyghur leader removed for China', and 'CIA and BND secretly owned Swiss cipher firm Crypto AG'.
items.would_show: A prosecution, parliamentary inquiry or internal investigation naming a serving officer of a national service who held a post on the staff of a multilateral body, or an inspection finding altered on a service's instruction.
items.would_refute: Vetting and counter-intelligence records at the main agencies showing officer placements were detected and refused, with the proved cases confined to the states that no longer exist in that form.
story: When a weapons inspectorate reports on a suspect site, or a relief agency counts the dead in a famine, the world treats the finding as neutral. It is neutral only if the people who produced it work for the organisation and nobody else. The probable position is that intelligence services are running officers under cover as ordinary staff inside United Nations agencies, inspectorates and relief bodies, because the access on offer is better than almost anything espionage can buy.

Both halves of this are already proved. A police spy for the apartheid government rose to become deputy director of an aid fund in Geneva. A Chinese official working inside the United Nations has said he arranged for a Uyghur leader to be removed from a UN forum at Beijing's request. And the appetite for sitting inside a trusted neutral institution is beyond doubt: the CIA and West Germany's BND secretly owned the Swiss company that sold cipher machines to around a hundred governments, and read what those governments wrote for decades.

The conditions could hardly be more favourable. These bodies recruit from member states and in practice often take the candidate a government puts forward. Vetting is light and belongs to the organisation, which has no counter-intelligence service of its own. Staff hold privileges and immunities, so the host country frequently cannot investigate them even when it suspects. And the names of the people who produce sensitive findings are withheld, for their own protection, which also means nobody outside can check who they are.

What would turn this into a case is a prosecution, a parliamentary inquiry or an internal investigation naming a serving officer of a national service on the staff of one of these bodies, or an inspection finding altered on a service's instruction.

items.title: Paid informants inside the movements that resist mines, pipelines and land seizures
items.claim: Companies and police forces are probably running paid informants and placed volunteers inside environmental, indigenous and land-defence movements in many countries, which would mean the groups opposing a project are reporting their own plans to the people they are opposing.
items.rule: The map proves that a company can get a state's intelligence apparatus working for it: a former head of French intelligence used state resources on behalf of a luxury goods group and was jailed for it. It also proves the reverse placement repeatedly, with movements putting their own people inside police and gendarmerie. What makes this version likely is the size of what a few days' warning is worth. A blockade, an injunction application or a leak timed to a financing deadline can cost a project hundreds of millions, so the value of knowing the plan in advance is enormous and the cost of a single informant is trivial.
items.conditions: These movements are open by necessity: they recruit volunteers, hold public meetings and need new people. There is no vetting. The handler is usually a private security contractor rather than a police officer, so the arrangement sits outside police accountability rules, and the contract between the company and the contractor is confidential commercial information. Where a protester is later charged, the state is not obliged to disclose a private informant.
items.documented: Proved on the map: 'France's former intelligence chief used state resources for LVMH and was jailed'. Honest gap: the map holds no case of an informant placed inside an environmental or indigenous movement, and the nearest cases run the other way, with movements placing members inside security forces.
items.would_show: A court record, inquiry or disclosure order naming a person who was inside such a movement while being paid by a company, a contractor or a police force, and reporting on it.
items.would_refute: Disclosure in the main protest prosecutions of recent years showing no informants were run inside the organising groups.
story: A mine, a pipeline or a plantation faces the same obstacle everywhere: a group of people who intend to stop it. Those groups are open by necessity. They hold public meetings, they need volunteers, and they vet nobody. The probable position is that companies and police forces are running paid informants inside environmental, indigenous and land-defence movements in many countries, so that the people opposing a project know its plans and the people making the plans are reporting them.

What makes it likely is arithmetic. A blockade timed to a financing deadline, an injunction filed the week before ground is broken, or a document leaked at the wrong moment can cost a project hundreds of millions. Against that, an informant costs almost nothing. The map already proves that a company can get a state's own intelligence machinery working on its behalf: a former head of French intelligence used state resources for a luxury goods group and went to prison for it.

The arrangement is also structurally hard to catch. The handler is usually a private security contractor rather than a serving police officer, which puts the whole thing outside police accountability rules, and the contract between the company and the contractor is confidential commercial information. When a protester is later prosecuted, the state has no obligation to disclose a privately run informant.

The map holds no case of this, and the cases it does hold run the other way, with movements placing their own members inside police forces and gendarmeries. What would turn it round is a court record, an inquiry or a disclosure order naming someone who sat inside such a movement while being paid by a company, a contractor or a police force to report on it.

items.title: States placing minders inside their own diasporas and the local politics around them
items.claim: States with large populations abroad are probably placing organisers and minders inside diaspora associations, student groups and local party politics in dozens of host countries, which would turn community bodies into instruments of a foreign government and reach local office through them.
items.rule: The map proves the shape in several host countries already, and in the receiving institutions rather than only in the community. A ruling party's cells are placed inside its own country's private companies. In Britain a security service publicly warned that a solicitor had covertly worked for a foreign state through members of parliament. In the United States a state governor's aide was charged with secretly acting for a foreign government, and in Australia a senator took a donor's money and then repeated that state's position. The method is the same in each: not an embassy making a request, but a person inside the association, the office or the party.
items.conditions: Community associations are private bodies with no disclosure duties, and the funding that reaches them crosses borders as ordinary remittance or sponsorship. Local politics is the cheapest point of entry anywhere: a council seat or a party branch can be influenced for the price of a few hundred memberships. Foreign agent registration laws, where they exist at all, mostly reach lobbyists and not community organisers, and intimidation inside a diaspora is rarely reported to the host country's police.
items.documented: Proved on the map: 'MI5 says Christine Lee covertly worked for China through MPs', 'Hochul aide Linda Sun charged with secretly working for China', 'Senator Sam Dastyari backed China's line after donor paid his bills', and 'Communist Party places its cells inside China's private companies'.
items.would_show: A prosecution, security service finding or parliamentary inquiry showing a person inside a diaspora association or a party branch acting on a foreign state's instruction, in a country where it has not yet been shown.
items.would_refute: Registration and security reviews in the main host countries finding the associations are self-organised, with the proved cases isolated rather than a method applied country by country.
story: Several states now have more people living outside their borders than many countries hold in total, and those populations organise themselves into associations, student societies and temple or church committees. The probable position is that the home governments are placing organisers and minders inside those bodies in dozens of host countries, and reaching into local politics through them, so that what looks like a community group is partly an arm of a foreign state.

This is proved often enough that the shape is not in question, and it is proved inside the receiving institutions rather than only in the community. Britain's security service publicly warned that a solicitor had worked covertly for a foreign state through members of parliament. In the United States, an aide to a state governor was charged with secretly acting for a foreign government. In Australia, a senator whose bills had been paid by a donor then repeated that state's position in public. And the same government places its party cells inside its own country's private companies, which is the method applied at home.

The gaps it moves through are wide. Community associations are private bodies with no duty to disclose anything, and money reaches them as ordinary sponsorship or remittance. Local politics is the cheapest entry point in any country: a council seat or a party branch can be swung by a few hundred memberships. Foreign agent laws, where they exist at all, were written for lobbyists rather than community organisers, and people pressured inside a diaspora very rarely report it to the local police.

What would extend this beyond the handful of countries where it is proved is a prosecution, a security service finding or a parliamentary inquiry showing the same thing - a person inside an association or a party branch acting on a foreign state's instruction - somewhere it has not yet been shown.

items.title: Sworn societies with undeclared members inside courts and police forces
items.claim: Sworn societies and closed fraternities probably still hold undeclared members among judges, prosecutors and senior police officers in many countries, which would mean cases are decided by people with an obligation to each other that nobody in the courtroom can see.
items.rule: This is among the most heavily proved shapes on the whole map, and the proof came from documents rather than allegation. A list recovered from one Italian lodge named 962 members across the state, including judges, prosecutors, police generals and intelligence chiefs. In South Africa a secret society counted five successive prime ministers among its members. In Turkey, a state that concluded a movement had taken its judiciary removed 2,745 judges in a single day and dismissed about 23,000 police officers. Nothing about the conditions that produced those cases has changed: the societies still exist, membership is still secret, and no judiciary in the world requires a judge to declare one.
items.conditions: Membership is sworn and concealed by design, so the only way it has ever surfaced is a seizure, a leak or a defector. Judicial recusal rules address family, money and prior involvement, not fraternal obligation, so a judge sharing a lodge with a party's lawyer is not required to say so. Police promotion panels are small and internal. Where a society is also a charity or a social club, its membership roll is legally private.
items.documented: Proved on the map: 'P2 membership list found: 962 names across Italy's state', the Broederbond cases naming five South African prime ministers as secret members, and the Turkish purges - '2,745 judges removed in one day over alleged Gulen membership' and 'About 23,000 police dismissed over alleged Gulen membership', which the map records with the state's claim attached rather than as a finding.
items.would_show: A recovered membership list, a disciplinary finding or a prosecution showing shared concealed membership between a judge or senior officer and a party before him, in a country and period not already on the map.
items.would_refute: Declaration regimes in the main judiciaries covering fraternal membership, published and audited, showing no concentration among judges and senior officers.
story: A judge hears a case. Somewhere in the room is a lawyer, a police witness or a defendant with whom he has sworn an oath of mutual obligation, in a society whose membership both men are bound to conceal. Nobody else present can know. The probable position is that sworn societies and closed fraternities still hold undeclared members among judges, prosecutors and senior police officers in many countries.

This is one of the best proved shapes on the entire map, and it was proved by documents rather than suspicion. A list recovered from an Italian lodge named 962 members spread across the state, judges, prosecutors, police generals and intelligence chiefs among them. In South Africa a secret society counted five consecutive prime ministers among its members. In Turkey a government that concluded a religious movement had captured its courts removed 2,745 judges in a single day and dismissed around 23,000 police officers, though the map records those as the state's own claim rather than as a proved finding.

What has not changed is any of the machinery that made those possible. Membership is sworn and hidden by design, so it has only ever come to light through a seizure, a leak or a defector. Recusal rules were written for family ties, money and prior involvement in a case, not for fraternal obligation, so a judge who shares a lodge with one side's counsel is under no duty to mention it. Police promotion panels are small and internal. And where a society registers as a charity or a social club, its membership roll is legally private.

What would carry this into the present is a recovered list, a disciplinary finding or a prosecution showing concealed shared membership between a judge or a senior officer and a party appearing before him, in a country and a period the map does not already hold.

items.title: Private armed contractors seated as advisers inside defence and interior ministries
items.claim: Private military and security companies are probably holding adviser's chairs inside the defence and interior ministries of many states, which would let a commercial armed force help decide the deployments, procurement and intelligence priorities it is then paid to carry out.
items.rule: The map proves this exactly once, and the single case is the template rather than an oddity: a man from a Russian private military company became the security adviser to the president of the Central African Republic, which placed the contractor inside the office that decides what the contractor does. The same shape is proved repeatedly through armed movements rather than companies, most sharply where a militia commander became a country's interior minister and where a city militia was converted wholesale into a state agency. The commercial version has grown fast in exactly the states with the weakest ministries, and an adviser's chair costs a company nothing next to the contracts it decides.
items.conditions: These appointments are often personal to a head of state rather than established posts, so they appear in no civil service register and carry no declaration of interest. The contracts the adviser helps shape are classified as national security matters. In several states the contractor is also paid in mining or oil concessions rather than cash, so the ministry's decisions touch the adviser's own revenue directly, and parliaments are not shown either side of the arrangement.
items.documented: Proved on the map: 'Wagner man Valery Zakharov becomes CAR president's security adviser'. The adjacent proved cases run through armed movements rather than firms - 'Badr's Qasim al-Araji became Iraq's interior minister and security adviser', and the Tripoli militia whose force was turned into a state agency.
items.would_show: A contractor's employee or former officer holding an advisory or decision-making post inside a defence or interior ministry in a second state, with a procurement, deployment or concession decision taken while he sat there.
items.would_refute: Ministry appointment records in the states where these companies operate showing the advisory posts are held by officials with no current or recent contractor employment.
story: A government hires a private armed company because its own forces cannot hold the country. Then someone from that company is given an office inside the ministry, with a title like security adviser to the president. From there he helps decide where troops go, what is bought and who is watched - the same questions whose answers his employer is paid to carry out. The probable position is that this arrangement now exists in a number of states rather than the one where it is proved.

That one case is the template. A man from a Russian private military company became security adviser to the president of the Central African Republic, which put the contractor inside the office that directs the contractor. The same shape is proved several times over on the map through armed movements rather than firms: a militia commander became Iraq's interior minister and security adviser, and in Libya a Tripoli militia chief had his force converted wholesale into a state agency.

The arrangement is nearly invisible by construction. These appointments are usually personal to a head of state rather than established civil service posts, so they appear in no staff register and require no declaration of interest. The contracts the adviser helps shape are classified as national security matters. And in several of these states the company is paid in mining or fuel concessions rather than money, so a ministry decision moves the adviser's own revenue, with no parliament shown either side of it.

What would make this a pattern rather than a single case is the same arrangement in a second state - a contractor's employee or former officer in an advisory or decision-making seat inside a defence or interior ministry, with a procurement, deployment or concession decided while he sat in it.

items.title: Ruling parties and security services placed inside companies that operate worldwide
items.claim: Ruling parties and state security services are probably placed inside companies that operate across dozens of countries, through cells, mandatory liaison officers or board seats held by serving officials, which would carry a government inside every market, port and network those companies run.
items.rule: The map proves the placement at home and the method abroad. A ruling communist party places its own cells inside its country's private companies, which is documented and official rather than alleged. A national security service took seats on the board of a state oil company, found by a United Nations panel of experts. And the map holds a long line of cases where a company's foreign operation carried a service inside it, including two intelligence agencies secretly owning the cipher firm that supplied a hundred governments. A company with cells or liaison officers at home does not shed them when it builds a port, a telecoms network or a data centre in another country.
items.conditions: The obligation is often lawful in the home country, which means it needs no concealment there and is simply never disclosed in the host country. Host state screening examines ownership and sometimes directors, but rarely internal party or security structures. Staff seconded this way hold ordinary commercial job titles. Where the company runs infrastructure, its own employees hold the administrative access, so no separate intrusion is needed.
items.documented: Proved on the map: 'Communist Party places its cells inside China's private companies', the South Sudan case placing the National Security Service on the state oil company's board, and 'CIA and BND secretly owned Swiss cipher firm Crypto AG' as the older form of a state inside a company that supplied the world.
items.would_show: A regulatory finding, prosecution or inquiry in a host country showing a party cell or a serving security officer inside the local operation of a foreign company, directing or reporting on it.
items.would_refute: Host country screening files on the main such companies showing their foreign subsidiaries carry no party or security structure, and that seconded staff hold no state position.
story: A company builds a port on one continent, a telecoms network on another and a data centre on a third. In its home country, the law requires it to host a cell of the ruling party, or to seat a liaison officer from the security service. Nothing in that obligation stops at the border. The probable position is that a number of companies operating in dozens of countries carry a government inside them, and carry it into every market they enter.

The home half of this is not alleged, it is official and documented: a ruling communist party places its own cells inside its country's private companies. The foreign half is proved too. A United Nations panel of experts found a national security service holding seats on the board of a state oil company. And the oldest version on the map is the starkest: two intelligence agencies secretly owned the Swiss firm that sold cipher machines to around a hundred governments, so that a company trusted worldwide was an instrument of two states for decades.

What makes it hard to see is that the arrangement is legal where it originates. It needs no concealment at home and is simply never mentioned abroad. Host country screening looks at ownership and sometimes at directors, but almost never at internal party or security structures, and people placed this way hold ordinary commercial job titles. Where the company runs infrastructure, its own staff already hold the administrative access, so nothing has to be broken into.

What would turn this into a case is a regulatory finding, a prosecution or an inquiry in a host country showing a party cell or a serving security officer inside the local operation of a foreign company, directing it or reporting on it.
